questions.stem: A 79 year old man with type 2 diabetes is found by his carer confused and drowsy after a week of increasing thirst. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 116 bpm, BP 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. His mucous membranes are dry. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Glucose >30, osmolality >320 and volume depletion without significant ketoacidosis (pH >7.3, HCO3- >15) is HHS.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.
Older type 2 diabetic, **days of thirst**, **confused**, **dry**: check glucose, osmolality and acid-base.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Glucose 44, osmolality 356, pH 7.36: HHS.

elim: pH and bicarbonate are near normal and ketones are minimal.
His glucose is extremely high.
There is no significant acidosis.
SIADH causes low sodium and low osmolality, not extreme hyperglycaemia.

steps.x: **B. Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state.** HHS triad: glucose >30, osmolality >320, volume depletion; pH >7.3 and HCO3- >15.

questions.stem: An 81 year old woman with type 2 diabetes controlled on metformin was started on furosemide 80 mg daily for heart failure 10 days ago. She is now drowsy and very dry. She has no fever, cough or urinary symptoms and has taken no new medicines other than this. Her glucose is 41 mmol/L and serum osmolality 348 mOsm/kg with a pH of 7.37.
questions.q: Which is the most likely precipitant of her condition?
questions.e: HHS is commonly triggered by infection, dehydration or drugs such as steroids and diuretics; high-dose furosemide started 10 days ago is the trigger.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.

clues: no fever, cough or urinary symptoms
steps.x: New **loop diuretic**, **no infection**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The diuretic.

elim: Heart failure itself causes overload, not this degree of dehydration.
Metformin has been taken safely; it does not cause HHS.
There is no chest pain or ECG change described.
She has no urinary symptoms or fever.

steps.x: **A. Furosemide.** HHS triggers: infection, dehydration, steroids, diuretics.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man with type 2 diabetes has 5 days of cough productive of green sputum, then increasing confusion. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. His glucose is 39 mmol/L, osmolality 342 mOsm/kg and pH 7.35. His chest X-ray (see item resources) is shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely precipitant of his hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state?
questions.e: Infection is the commonest HHS trigger; right lower zone consolidation with fever and sputum is pneumonia, which must be treated alongside the HHS.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.
Fever, **green sputum** and a **focal opacity**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Pneumonia triggered the HHS.

elim: Oedema is bilateral and perihilar, not a single zone with fever.
A mass would not explain fever and green sputum over 5 days.
There is no visible lung edge.
PE does not cause focal consolidation with green sputum.

steps.x: **E. Right lower lobe pneumonia.** Always look for and treat the trigger: infection first.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man with type 2 diabetes has 3 days of thirst and confusion. This morning he had an hour of central chest heaviness. His pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 100/64 mmHg. His glucose is 47 mmol/L and serum osmolality 351 mOsm/kg. Troponin is raised. His ECG (see item resources) is shown.

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: ST elevation in II, III and aVF with reciprocal depression in I and aVL.

questions.q: Which is the most likely precipitant or associated event to treat?
questions.e: MI can precipitate HHS (and hyperviscosity raises MI risk); ST elevation in II, III and aVF with reciprocal change is an inferior STEMI that needs urgent treatment.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.
Chest heaviness, **troponin up**, **ST elevation** in the inferior leads.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Inferior STEMI.

elim: The ST elevation is in II, III and aVF, not V1–V4.
Hyperkalaemia gives peaked T waves, not regional ST elevation.
Pericarditis gives widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation without reciprocal change.
PE gives sinus tachycardia or right heart strain, not inferior ST elevation.

steps.x: **C. Inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction.** Treat the precipitant: infection, MI, stroke.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman with type 2 diabetes has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure at home. She has no history of epilepsy. Her family say she has been drinking constantly and passing large volumes of urine for a week, and has been weak and drowsy. Her pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 98/62 mmHg. A CT head is normal. Her glucose is 52 mmol/L and pH 7.36.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her seizure?
questions.e: A week of polyuria, polydipsia, weakness and drowsiness then a seizure, with glucose 52 and a normal pH, is HHS.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.

clues: drinking constantly and passing large volumes of urine
steps.x: **Polyuria, polydipsia**, drowsy, **glucose 52**, normal pH.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: HHS causing seizures.

elim: Nothing suggests alcohol use.
Her glucose is very high.
The CT head is normal.
New-onset epilepsy at 68 with this metabolic picture is unlikely.

steps.x: **B. Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state.** HHS can present with seizures as well as confusion.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman with type 2 diabetes is drowsy and dehydrated after 6 days of diarrhoea. Her pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 94/58 mmHg. Investigations: glucose 38 mmol/L (4.0–7.8), serum osmolality 338 mOsm/kg (275–295), venous pH 7.32 (7.35–7.45), bicarbonate 19 mmol/L (22–29), blood ketones 1.0 mmol/L (<0.6).
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis from diarrhoea
questions.e: Despite mild ketosis and a slightly low pH, pH >7.3 and HCO3- >15 with glucose >30 and osmolality >320 is HHS; the absence of significant acidosis separates it from DKA.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.
Slightly low pH but **above 7.3**, HCO3- **above 15**, osmolality **above 320**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Not significant acidosis: HHS.

elim: DKA needs ketones ≥3 mmol/L with pH <7.3 or HCO3- <15; hers are milder.
Glucose is 38, not normal.
Glucose 38 and osmolality 338 are a diabetic emergency.
The mild acidosis does not explain the hyperosmolar state.

steps.x: **D. Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state.** HHS: pH >7.3, HCO3- >15. A little ketosis is allowed.

questions.stem: An 84 year old man with no known medical history is brought in by his son with 10 days of thirst, passing large volumes of urine and worsening confusion. He is overweight and has not seen a doctor for years. His pulse rate is 120 bpm and BP 88/50 mmHg. His glucose is 56 mmol/L, osmolality 370 mOsm/kg, pH 7.38 and ketones 0.3 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Diabetic ketoacidosis with new type 1 diabetes
Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state with previously undiagnosed type 2 diabetes
questions.e: HHS occurs in type 2 diabetes and can be its first presentation, typically in older people after days to weeks of polyuria and polydipsia.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.
Older, overweight, **no known diabetes**, gradual onset, **no ketones**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: HHS as the first sign of type 2 diabetes.

elim: DI causes polyuria with a normal glucose.
Ketones are absent and pH is normal.
Calcium can cause polyuria, but this glucose explains everything.
That causes low osmolality, not 370.

steps.x: **D. Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state with previously undiagnosed type 2 diabetes.** HHS is the type 2 emergency and may be the first presentation.

questions.stem: A 77 year old woman is on day 2 of treatment for HHS. Her osmolality has fallen gradually from 362 to 318 mOsm/kg. This morning she has sudden weakness of her right arm and leg and difficulty finding words. Her capillary glucose is 14 mmol/L and sodium 144 mmol/L (135–145).
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her new symptoms?
questions.e: Hyperosmolar states predispose to hyperviscosity and thrombosis, raising the risk of stroke, MI and VTE.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.

clues: sudden weakness of her right arm and leg
steps.x: **Sudden focal** deficit, gradual correction, normal glucose and sodium.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Thrombotic stroke.

elim: Her osmolality fell gradually, and oedema causes global drowsiness, not a focal deficit.
There is no fever, and the deficit is focal rather than global.
There has been no fall, and the onset was sudden.
There has been no seizure.

steps.x: **B. Ischaemic stroke.** HHS complications: cerebral oedema (too fast) and thrombosis (stroke, MI, VTE).

questions.stem: An 86 year old woman with type 2 diabetes is brought from her care home after a week of poor oral intake and increasing sleepiness. Her glucose is 48 mmol/L, serum osmolality 365 mOsm/kg and venous pH 7.37. Her pulse rate is 122 bpm and BP 86/50 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Dry mucous membranes and a reduced GCS
questions.e: Profound volume depletion in HHS gives dry mucous membranes, hypotension, tachycardia and a reduced GCS.

steps.x: A 'most likely finding' question: decide whether the patient is acidotic and whether they are dry.
**Normal pH** (no Kussmaul, no ketone breath), **dry**, **sleepy**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Dehydration and reduced consciousness.

elim: She is profoundly volume depleted, not overloaded.
Kussmaul breathing is a sign of DKA acidosis; her pH is normal.
Acetone breath means ketosis, which is absent in HHS.
Oedema suggests overload, not dehydration.

steps.x: **C. Dry mucous membranes and a reduced GCS.** HHS signs: dry mucous membranes, low BP, tachycardia, reduced GCS. No Kussmaul breathing.

questions.stem: An 88 year old man with dementia and type 2 diabetes lives alone. During a heatwave he has barely drunk for 4 days. His neighbour finds him confused. He has no fever, cough or urinary symptoms and takes no new medicines. His glucose is 42 mmol/L, osmolality 352 mOsm/kg and pH 7.38.
questions.q: Which is the most likely precipitant of his condition?
questions.e: Dehydration (here a heatwave with poor intake in dementia) is a classic HHS trigger and is worsened by the osmotic diuresis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.

clues: no fever, cough or urinary symptoms
steps.x: **Heatwave**, **not drinking**, no infection, no new drugs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Dehydration.

elim: He takes no new medicines.
There is no chest pain or ECG change.
He is not on steroids.
He has no fever or urinary symptoms.

steps.x: **A. Dehydration.** Triggers: infection, dehydration, steroids, diuretics.

questions.stem: An 82 year old woman is on day 3 of treatment for HHS. She has been bed-bound since admission and her VTE prophylaxis was missed. She develops sudden breathlessness and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Her pulse rate is 124 bpm, BP 104/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88% breathing air. Her chest is clear.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Hyperosmolarity causes hyperviscosity and thrombosis; with immobility and missed prophylaxis, sudden pleuritic pain, hypoxia and a clear chest suggest PE.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.
**Hypercoagulable** HHS, **immobile**, **no prophylaxis**, sudden hypoxia, clear chest.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: PE.

elim: Her chest is clear, with no crackles.
Pneumonia gives fever and focal signs over hours to days.
This causes drowsiness, not chest pain.
Nothing suggests a pneumothorax and breath sounds are normal.

steps.x: **E. Pulmonary embolism.** HHS = hyperviscous: VTE, stroke and MI risk.

questions.stem: A 75 year old man with type 2 diabetes is confused and dehydrated. His pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 94/60 mmHg. Investigations: sodium 150 mmol/L (135–145), glucose 46 mmol/L (4.0–7.8), urea 20 mmol/L (2.5–7.8), venous pH 7.36 (7.35–7.45). The laboratory osmolality is not yet available.
questions.q: Which is his estimated serum osmolality?
questions.e: Osmolality ≈ (2 × Na) + glucose + urea = 300 + 46 + 20 = 366 mOsm/kg, well above the 320 threshold for HHS.

steps.x: A calculation question: write the formula before you look at the options.
Use **(2 × Na) + glucose + urea**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: This forgets to double the sodium.
This doubles sodium but leaves out glucose and urea.
This leaves out urea.
This doubles the glucose as well.

steps.x: **D. 366 mOsm/kg.** Estimated osmolality = 2Na + glucose + urea; HHS if >320.

questions.stem: A 78 year old woman with type 2 diabetes is brought in confused with a capillary glucose of 38 mmol/L. She has had a cough for 4 days. Her temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 110 bpm and BP 96/58 mmHg. IV access has been obtained and a capillary ketone level is 0.5 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial set of blood tests?
o: U&Es, venous blood gas, FBC and CRP
questions.e: First-line bloods in HHS are U&Es, VBG/ABG and FBC/CRP to assess electrolytes, acid-base status and an infective trigger.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what you need to know and which test answers it.
Need **electrolytes**, **acid-base** and evidence of **infection**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: U&Es, VBG, FBC, CRP.

elim: These guide long-term care, not the emergency.
These do not assess electrolytes, acid-base or infection.
These are not first-line in HHS.
Only if the history suggests MI or VTE.

steps.x: **E. U&Es, venous blood gas, FBC and CRP.** HHS first bloods: U&Es, VBG/ABG, FBC/CRP.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with type 2 diabetes is drowsy with a glucose of 44 mmol/L. His serum osmolality is 344 mOsm/kg. The registrar wants to confirm that this is HHS rather than DKA before deciding on insulin.
questions.q: Which result would best support HHS?
o: Blood ketones 0.4 mmol/L with venous pH 7.36
Blood ketones 4.8 mmol/L with venous pH 7.12
questions.e: Minimal or absent ketones with a normal or only mildly low pH confirm the absence of significant acidosis, the feature that separates HHS from DKA.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what you need to know and which test answers it.
Both have high glucose; the difference is **acidosis and ketones**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Low ketones, normal pH.

elim: This is DKA.
Both DKA and HHS can have a very high glucose.
This suggests infection but does not separate them.
Sodium does not distinguish the two.

steps.x: **A. Blood ketones 0.4 mmol/L with venous pH 7.36.** HHS vs DKA: check ketones and pH, not glucose.

questions.stem: A 73 year old woman is 3 hours into treatment for HHS with IV 0.9% saline. On admission her glucose was 49 mmol/L and osmolality 362 mOsm/kg. Her nurse asks which measurement, repeated hourly at first, best tells the team whether correction is happening at a safe rate.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to monitor?
questions.e: Correction in HHS must be gradual; serum osmolality (measured or 2Na + glucose + urea) is tracked to make sure it falls slowly.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what you need to know and which test answers it.
**Safe rate** of correction = how fast osmolality falls.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Osmolality.

elim: Ketones are minimal in HHS and guide DKA, not HHS.
Lactate does not reflect osmolar correction.
HbA1c reflects 3-month control.
Urine glucose does not quantify osmolar shifts.

steps.x: **D. Serum osmolality.** Monitor osmolality in HHS; ketones in DKA.

questions.stem: An 80 year old man with type 2 diabetes is admitted with HHS. He has had burning on passing urine and new incontinence for 3 days. His temperature is 38.4°C. His glucose is 40 mmol/L and osmolality 346 mOsm/kg. U&Es and a venous blood gas have been sent.
questions.q: Which other investigation is most useful to identify the precipitant?
questions.e: Infection is the commonest trigger; FBC and CRP (with cultures) identify and track it so it can be treated.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what you need to know and which test answers it.
Fever with **urinary symptoms**: look for infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Infection markers and urine culture.

elim: There is no focal neurology; infection is the likely trigger.
Nothing suggests endocarditis or heart failure.
This shows chronic control, not the trigger.
Adrenal failure is not suggested.

steps.x: **C. FBC, CRP and urine culture.** Find and treat the trigger: FBC/CRP and cultures for infection.

questions.stem: An 83 year old woman with type 2 diabetes is drowsy and dehydrated. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm and BP 90/54 mmHg. Investigations: glucose 51 mmol/L (4.0–7.8), osmolality 368 mOsm/kg (275–295), venous pH 7.35, ketones 0.5 mmol/L (<0.6), potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5–5.3). IV access has been obtained.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: 1 litre of 0.9% sodium chloride over 1–2 hours
questions.e: IV fluids come first in HHS: 0.9% saline, e.g. 1 litre over 1–2 hours, before insulin.

steps.x: A management question: work out the severity and the stage of treatment first.
**Dehydrated** and hypotensive, **no ketosis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Fluids first.

elim: She is profoundly hyperglycaemic.
Insulin comes after fluid resuscitation, and HHS uses a lower dose.
She is not acidotic.
Insulin is not the first step, and basal insulin will not treat the emergency.

steps.x: **A. 1 litre of 0.9% sodium chloride over 1–2 hours.** HHS: 0.9% saline first; insulin only once fluid-resuscitated.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man with HHS has just received his first litre of 0.9% saline. His glucose is 45 mmol/L (from 48), osmolality 350 mOsm/kg and ketones 0.3 mmol/L. His BP is 96/60 mmHg and he is still clinically dry. A junior doctor asks whether to start insulin now.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate plan for insulin?
o: Give a 10-unit intravenous insulin bolus now
Start fixed-rate insulin at 0.1 units/kg/hour now
questions.e: Fluids alone lower osmolality and glucose; low-dose IV insulin is only started once fully fluid-resuscitated (or if glucose stops falling).

steps.x: A management question: work out the severity and the stage of treatment first.
Glucose already **falling with fluids**, still **dry**, **no ketones**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Not yet: more fluid first.

elim: Boluses cause rapid osmolar shifts and are not used.
This is the DKA regimen; in HHS fluids come first.
Oral agents have no place in the acute emergency.
This is not how HHS is treated.

steps.x: **E. Withhold insulin until fully fluid-resuscitated.** Fluids before insulin in HHS; insulin is low-dose and later.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman with HHS has had 4 litres of 0.9% saline over 10 hours and is now well perfused. Her glucose has plateaued at 30 mmol/L. The team plans to start low-dose IV insulin. Investigations: potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5–5.3), sodium 147 mmol/L (135–145).
questions.q: Which is the most important additional step?
o: Add potassium chloride to the intravenous fluids
questions.e: Electrolytes, particularly potassium, must be corrected alongside insulin, which drives potassium into cells.

steps.x: A management question: work out the severity and the stage of treatment first.
Insulin about to start with **potassium already low**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Replace potassium.

elim: This is for hyperkalaemia with ECG changes.
She is not acidotic.
She still needs fluid as insulin starts.
Glucose comes later, and she needs potassium.

steps.x: **A. Add potassium chloride to the intravenous fluids.** Low-dose insulin once resuscitated; correct potassium alongside.

questions.stem: An 82 year old man with type 2 diabetes is being treated for HHS with IV 0.9% saline. He has a 3 day history of a hot, red, swollen left leg spreading from a foot ulcer. His temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 102/64 mmHg. His CRP is 214 mg/L (<5).
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Treating the underlying precipitant (infection, MI, stroke) is part of HHS management; here cellulitis needs IV antibiotics.

steps.x: A management question: work out the severity and the stage of treatment first.
**Infected leg** with fever and high CRP: the **trigger**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Treat the infection.

elim: He is not acidotic.
Oral agents are not part of acute HHS management.
He still needs fluid resuscitation.
The leg is hot and red from an ulcer with fever, typical of cellulitis.

steps.x: **A. Intravenous antibiotics for cellulitis.** Treat the precipitant: infection, MI, stroke.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman with HHS has received IV 0.9% saline and low-dose insulin. Over 4 hours her osmolality has fallen from 364 to 330 mOsm/kg and her glucose from 50 to 22 mmol/L. She is alert and her GCS is 15. The guideline target is a fall of 3–8 mOsm/kg per hour.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Continue treatment but slow the rate of correction
questions.e: Osmolality has fallen about 8.5 mOsm/kg per hour, faster than the JBDS target; correction must be gradual to avoid cerebral oedema.

steps.x: A management question: work out the severity and the stage of treatment first.
34 over 4 hours ≈ **8.5 per hour**: **too fast**, but **no oedema yet**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Slow down.

elim: Hypertonic saline is for established cerebral oedema; she is alert.
This would speed correction further.
Correction is already too fast.
Mannitol is for cerebral oedema, which has not developed.

steps.x: **B. Continue treatment but slow the rate of correction.** Gradual correction throughout; too fast risks cerebral oedema.

questions.stem: An 80 year old woman with type 2 diabetes is admitted with HHS (glucose 46 mmol/L, osmolality 358 mOsm/kg). She is started on IV 0.9% saline. She has no history of bleeding and her platelet count and renal function are acceptable. She is likely to be bed-bound for several days.
questions.q: Which additional treatment should be prescribed?
questions.e: Hyperosmolar states predispose to hyperviscosity and thrombosis (stroke, MI, VTE), so HHS patients need prophylactic LMWH unless contraindicated.

steps.x: A management question: work out the severity and the stage of treatment first.
**Hyperosmolar** and **immobile**: very high VTE risk.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Prophylactic LMWH.

elim: There is no stroke or MI to treat.
Antiplatelets do not prevent VTE.
Pharmacological prophylaxis is needed given her high risk.
Full anticoagulation is not needed without a clot.

steps.x: **B. Prophylactic low molecular weight heparin.** HHS is pro-thrombotic: give VTE prophylaxis.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man with type 1 diabetes has glucose 28 mmol/L, ketones 5.4 mmol/L and pH 7.09. In the next bay, a 79 year old woman with type 2 diabetes has glucose 52 mmol/L, ketones 0.4 mmol/L and pH 7.37. A student asks why she is not acidotic despite a higher glucose.
questions.q: Which best explains the difference?
o: Her kidneys excrete ketones more efficiently
Her liver cannot make ketones with age
Residual insulin suppresses lipolysis but not hyperglycaemia
She has an absolute insulin deficiency
questions.e: In HHS, relative rather than absolute insulin deficiency leaves enough insulin to suppress lipolysis and ketogenesis, but not enough to prevent severe hyperglycaemia; in DKA deficiency is near-absolute.

steps.x: A science question comparing two patients: decide what differs between them.
Same problem (high glucose), but **only one makes ketones**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Relative vs absolute insulin deficiency.

elim: Ketones are not being made in the first place.
Ageing does not stop ketogenesis.
That is the DKA patient; she has relative deficiency.
There is insulin resistance, but she is still relatively deficient.

steps.x: **C. Residual insulin suppresses lipolysis but not hyperglycaemia.** A little insulin stops ketones; it takes more to control glucose.

questions.stem: A 81 year old woman with type 2 diabetes has had 10 days of polyuria. Her glucose has risen from 25 to 54 mmol/L over 3 days even though she has eaten very little. Her urea is 24 mmol/L (2.5–7.8) and creatinine 196 µmol/L (45–90; 90 a month ago). Her urine output has now fallen.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason her glucose has continued to rise?
o: Pre-renal impairment reducing renal glucose excretion
Rising renal glucose threshold from alcohol
questions.e: Osmotic diuresis causes dehydration and hypovolaemia with pre-renal impairment, so less glucose is excreted and hyperglycaemia worsens: a self-reinforcing cycle.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind what the stem describes.
Polyuria → **dry** → **kidneys failing** → glucose cannot get out.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A vicious cycle via pre-renal AKI.

elim: She has eaten very little.
Ketones are minimal in HHS.
Insulin lowers glucose.
Nothing suggests alcohol.

steps.x: **D. Pre-renal impairment reducing renal glucose excretion.** Osmotic diuresis → dehydration → pre-renal AKI → less glucose excreted → higher glucose.

questions.stem: A 78 year old man with HHS had an osmolality of 372 mOsm/kg on admission. After rapid fluid and insulin treatment it fell to 318 mOsm/kg within 5 hours. He became drowsy with a headache and vomited. A CT head shows diffuse cerebral swelling. ITU is contacted about mannitol and hypertonic saline.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his deterioration?
o: Haemorrhage into the brain from hypertension
Hyperviscosity causing a large vessel stroke
Rapid shift of water into brain cells
questions.e: High osmolality draws water out of brain cells; rapid correction causes an equally rapid osmotic shift of water back in, precipitating cerebral oedema.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind what the stem describes.

clues: drowsy with a headache and vomited
steps.x: **Fast fall** in osmolality then **drowsy**, headache, diffuse swelling.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Water rushing back into brain cells.

elim: CT shows diffuse swelling, not blood.
That gives a focal deficit and a territorial infarct.
Hypoglycaemia does not cause diffuse swelling on CT.
That happens at presentation; correction moves water back in.

steps.x: **D. Rapid shift of water into brain cells.** Too-rapid correction → water moves into brain cells → cerebral oedema.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man with HHS develops chest pain on day 2. His ECG shows new ST depression in V4–V6 and troponin is rising. His osmolality on admission was 368 mOsm/kg and his haematocrit is raised. He had no previous cardiac history.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism linking HHS with this event?
questions.e: Hyperosmolar states predispose to hyperviscosity and thrombosis, explaining the increased risk of MI, stroke and VTE.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind what the stem describes.
Very **concentrated blood** (high osmolality, high haematocrit), then **MI**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Thick blood clots.

elim: Vasospasm is not the recognised mechanism.
There is no arrhythmia or high potassium described.
Ketones are minimal in HHS.
There is no viral illness; this is ischaemia.

steps.x: **C. Hyperviscosity predisposing to thrombosis.** HHS: hyperviscosity → stroke, MI, VTE.

questions.stem: A 77 year old woman with HHS receives 3 litres of IV 0.9% saline over 6 hours and no insulin. Her glucose falls from 48 to 33 mmol/L and her osmolality from 360 to 336 mOsm/kg. Her urine output improves and her BP rises from 88/50 to 116/70 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the fall in glucose?
o: Dilution and restored renal glucose excretion
Glucose entering cells via the sodium-glucose cotransporter
Hepatic glycogen storage stimulated by sodium
Increased insulin secretion caused by saline
questions.e: IV fluids correct the dehydration from osmotic diuresis, diluting glucose and restoring renal perfusion so glucose is excreted, which reduces serum osmolality.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind what the stem describes.
Glucose falls **without insulin** as she is **rehydrated** and **passes urine**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Dilution and renal excretion.

elim: Saline does not stimulate insulin release.
Saline does not drive cellular glucose uptake.
Sodium does not trigger glycogen storage.
Ketones are minimal in HHS.

steps.x: **A. Dilution and restored renal glucose excretion.** Fluids alone lower osmolality and glucose in HHS, which is why they come first.

questions.stem: An 85 year old man with type 2 diabetes is brought in after 8 days of polyuria, thirst and increasing confusion. He is very dry, with a pulse rate of 120 bpm and BP 86/52 mmHg. He is breathing quietly at 18 breaths per minute and there is no ketotic smell. Blood results are awaited.
questions.q: Which set of results is most likely?
o: Glucose 2.1 mmol/L, osmolality 290 mOsm/kg, pH 7.40, HCO3- 24 mmol/L
Glucose 26 mmol/L, osmolality 310 mOsm/kg, pH 7.08, HCO3- 8 mmol/L
Glucose 50 mmol/L, osmolality 365 mOsm/kg, pH 7.36, HCO3- 24 mmol/L
Glucose 8 mmol/L, osmolality 262 mOsm/kg, pH 7.40, HCO3- 25 mmol/L
Glucose 9 mmol/L, osmolality 296 mOsm/kg, pH 7.21, HCO3- 12 mmol/L
questions.e: A gradual, days-long illness in type 2 diabetes with profound dehydration, confusion and no Kussmaul breathing fits HHS: glucose >30, osmolality >320, pH >7.3 and HCO3- >15.

steps.x: A 'most likely results' question: predict the diagnosis, then its numbers.
Gradual onset, **no Kussmaul**, **no ketones** on the breath, very dry.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Very high glucose and osmolality, normal pH.

elim: This is hypoglycaemia.
This is DKA, with Kussmaul breathing and ketotic breath.
Low osmolality suggests hyponatraemia.
This is a metabolic acidosis without hyperglycaemia.

steps.x: **C. Glucose 50 mmol/L, osmolality 365 mOsm/kg, pH 7.36, HCO3- 24 mmol/L.** HHS: glucose >30, osmolality >320, pH >7.3, HCO3- >15.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman with type 2 diabetes and a brain tumour was started on dexamethasone 16 mg daily 8 days ago. She has become increasingly thirsty and drowsy. Her pulse rate is 114 bpm and BP 94/60 mmHg. Her glucose is 43 mmol/L, osmolality 349 mOsm/kg, venous pH 7.36 and ketones 0.4 mmol/L. A CT head is unchanged.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Raised intracranial pressure from tumour growth
questions.e: High-dose steroids are a recognised HHS trigger; glucose >30, osmolality >320 and normal pH make the diagnosis, which is clinical and biochemical.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.
New **high-dose steroid**, then thirst and drowsiness with the HHS numbers.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Steroid-triggered HHS.

elim: She is on high-dose steroids, and adrenal crisis causes hypoglycaemia.
Ketones are minimal and pH is normal.
CT head is unchanged.
SIADH gives low osmolality, not 349.

steps.x: **D. Steroid-induced hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state.** Steroids and diuretics are drug triggers for HHS.
